en: Fermions, Dirac Matrices, and the Dirac Sea

p.src: The Dirac sea is our destination, but the route matters. Before facing negative energy in the relativistic electron theory, we need two pieces of machinery. First comes the operator algebra that distinguishes fermions from bosons. Then comes a review of the one-dimensional Dirac equation, where every enlargement of the wavefunction can be seen without the geometry of three spatial dimensions. Once those pieces are in place, the three-dimensional equation will force its own matrix structure, and the opening discussion of filled and empty fermion states will return as the key to positrons.

u.src: Exchange Becomes Operator Algebra
en: Exchange Becomes Operator Algebra

p.src:
Consider two identical particles, one at $x$ and one at $y$. The labels $x$ and $y$ denote complete positions; they are not two Cartesian coordinates of a single particle. Acting on the vacuum with two creation operators gives $\lvert x,y\rangle
=
\psi^\dagger(x)\psi^\dagger(y)\lvert0\rangle.$

en:
Consider two identical particles, one at $x$ and one at $y$. The labels $x$ and $y$ denote complete positions; they are not two Cartesian coordinates of a single particle. Acting on the vacuum with two creation operators gives $\lvert x,y\rangle
=
\psi^\dagger(x)\psi^\dagger(y)\lvert0\rangle.$

p.src:
For bosons, exchanging the two slots leaves the state unchanged: $\lvert x,y\rangle=\lvert y,x\rangle.$ The operator statement that guarantees this symmetry is $\psi^\dagger(x)\psi^\dagger(y)
=
\psi^\dagger(y)\psi^\dagger(x).$ Two bosonic creation operators commute, so we may reverse their order without changing the state they create.

en:
For bosons, exchanging the two slots leaves the state unchanged: $\lvert x,y\rangle=\lvert y,x\rangle.$ The operator statement that guarantees this symmetry is $\psi^\dagger(x)\psi^\dagger(y)
=
\psi^\dagger(y)\psi^\dagger(x).$ Two bosonic creation operators commute, so we may reverse their order without changing the state they create.

p.src:
For fermions, exchange changes the sign: $\lvert x,y\rangle=-\lvert y,x\rangle.$ The overall sign of an isolated state vector is not observable, but relative signs between alternatives are observable, so this minus sign must be carried consistently. Equation  requires $\psi^\dagger(x)\psi^\dagger(y)
=
-\,\psi^\dagger(y)\psi^\dagger(x).$

p.src: For any two operators $A$ and $B$, define the anti-commutator by $\{A,B\}:=AB+BA.$ The exchange rule is therefore $\{\psi^\dagger(x),\psi^\dagger(y)\}=0.$ The corresponding fermionic field algebra replaces the bosonic commutators by anti-commutators. One must keep two uses of the word distinct: field operators anti-commute because of Fermi statistics, while matrices will later anti-commute in order to cancel cross terms in a relativistic dispersion relation.

p.src:
Now set $y=x$ in Eq. . Both products become the same: $\begin{aligned}
0
&=\{\psi^\dagger(x),\psi^\dagger(x)\}\\
&=2\,\psi^\dagger(x)\psi^\dagger(x).\end{aligned}$ Hence $\bigl(\psi^\dagger(x)\bigr)^2=0.$ Trying to create two identical fermions in the same one-particle state gives the zero vector. That is the exclusion principle in operator form.

u.src: Why Filled and Empty Are Symmetric for a Fermion
en: Why Filled and Empty Are Symmetric for a Fermion

p.src:
There is a second difference between bosonic and fermionic operators, subtler than exclusion and essential later. For a single bosonic mode, $=1,
\qquad
n=0,1,2,\ldots.$ Interchanging $a$ and $a^\dagger$ changes the sign of the commutator. Even if the operators were merely called $A$ and $B$, the algebra would tell us which ordering raises the occupation number and which lowers it.

p.src:
The bosonic occupation ladder also has an orientation. The annihilation operator eventually reaches $\lvert0\rangle$ and gives zero, whereas the creation operator can continue indefinitely: $\begin{aligned}
a\lvert0\rangle&=0,\\
a^\dagger\lvert n\rangle&\propto\lvert n+1\rangle,
\qquad n=0,1,2,\ldots.\end{aligned}$ Turning this ladder upside down does not reproduce the same spectrum. There is a bottom but no top.

p.src:
For one fermionic mode, $\{a,a^\dagger\}=1,
\qquad
a^2=(a^\dagger)^2=0,
\qquad
n=0,1.$ The creation operator takes the empty state to the filled state and then stops: $a^\dagger\lvert0\rangle=\lvert1\rangle,
\qquad
a^\dagger\lvert1\rangle=0.$ The annihilation operator performs the reverse: $a\lvert1\rangle=\lvert0\rangle,
\qquad
a\lvert0\rangle=0.$ There are only two states, so the diagram is symmetric under interchanging filled with empty and $a$ with $a^\dagger$. The operators still have different physical meanings, but their algebra no longer singles out one as creation and the other as annihilation. This formal symmetry is the seed of the particle-hole reinterpretation.

p.src: The One-Dimensional Dirac Construction

u.src: The One-Dimensional Dirac Construction
en: The One-Dimensional Dirac Construction

p.src: Return now to one particle in one spatial dimension. The simplest first-order relativistic wave equation is $i\partial_t\psi=-\,i\partial_x\psi.$ With $P=-i\partial_x$, this is $H=P.$ A momentum eigenstate has $E=p$, and its group velocity is $v_g=\frac{dE}{dp}=1.$ Positive or negative momentum, and therefore positive or negative energy, still gives a wave moving rigidly to the right. The sign of $p$ changes the phase pattern, not the propagation direction.

p.src:
A massive particle must be able to move in either direction. Introduce a second component satisfying $H\psi_1=P\psi_1,
\qquad
H\psi_2=-P\psi_2.$ The first component moves right; the second moves left. Put them into a column, $\Psi=
\begin{pmatrix}
\psi_1\\
\psi_2
\end{pmatrix},$ and define $\alpha=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&0\\
0&-1
\end{pmatrix}.$ Both equations become $H\Psi=\alpha P\Psi.$ The cost of including both directions is a new two-valued internal degree of freedom.

p.src:
Direction alone does not produce mass. Introduce a second matrix, $\beta=
\begin{pmatrix}
0&1\\
1&0
\end{pmatrix},$ and try $H=\alpha P+\beta m.$ The matrices satisfy $\alpha^2=\beta^2=\mathbb{1},
\qquad
\{\alpha,\beta\}=0.$ Squaring the Hamiltonian gives $\begin{aligned}
H^2
&=(\alpha P+\beta m)^2\\
&=\alpha^2P^2+\beta^2m^2
  +(\alpha\beta+\beta\alpha)Pm\\
&=P^2+m^2.
\end{aligned}$ The anti-commutator in Eq.  removes the unwanted term linear in both $P$ and $m$.

p.src: The off-diagonal matrix $\beta$ couples the two directional components. It is useful to picture the mass term as continually mixing right-moving and left-moving amplitudes. The picture should not be literalized into a particle bouncing back and forth along a microscopic track, but it captures why a massive wavepacket can have an average speed below light and can possess a rest frame, whereas an isolated massless chiral component cannot.

p.src:
In three spatial dimensions momentum is a vector. A Hamiltonian linear in momentum and rotationally scalar therefore suggests another vector, now a vector whose components are matrices: $H=\boldsymbol{\alpha}\cdot\mathbf P
=\alpha_xP_x+\alpha_yP_y+\alpha_zP_z.$

en:
In three spatial dimensions momentum is a vector. A Hamiltonian linear in momentum and rotationally scalar therefore suggests another vector, now a vector whose components are matrices: $H=\boldsymbol{\alpha}\cdot\mathbf P
=\alpha_xP_x+\alpha_yP_y+\alpha_zP_z.$

p.src: The three-dimensional massless ansatz $H=\boldsymbol{\alpha}\cdot\mathbf P$ at the point where one matrix becomes a vector of three matrices.

u.src: The three-dimensional massless ansatz $H=\boldsymbol{\alpha}\cdot\mathbf P$ at the point where one matrix becomes a vector of three matrices.

caption.en: The three-dimensional massless ansatz $H=\boldsymbol{\alpha}\cdot\mathbf P$ at the point where one matrix becomes a vector of three matrices.

p.src:
Begin again with the massless case. We require $H^2=\mathbf P^2=P_x^2+P_y^2+P_z^2.$ Expanding the square of Eq. , $\begin{aligned}
H^2
&=\alpha_x^2P_x^2+\alpha_y^2P_y^2\\
&\quad+\alpha_z^2P_z^2\\
&\quad+\{\alpha_x,\alpha_y\}P_xP_y\\
&\quad+\{\alpha_x,\alpha_z\}P_xP_z\\
&\quad+\{\alpha_y,\alpha_z\}P_yP_z.\end{aligned}$ The diagonal terms are correct if $\alpha_x^2=\alpha_y^2=\alpha_z^2=\mathbb{1},$ and all cross terms disappear if $\{\alpha_i,\alpha_j\}=0,
\qquad i\ne j.$

p.src:
Three familiar $2\times2$ matrices do exactly this: $\sigma_x=
\begin{pmatrix}
0&1\\
1&0
\end{pmatrix},
\quad
\sigma_y=
\begin{pmatrix}
0&-i\\
i&0
\end{pmatrix},
\quad
\sigma_z=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&0\\
0&-1
\end{pmatrix}.$ Thus one solution is $\alpha_i=\sigma_i,
\qquad
H=\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\mathbf P.$

p.src:
For a momentum eigenstate, $\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\mathbf p
=
|\mathbf p|\,\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\widehat{\mathbf p}.$ The operator $\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\widehat{\mathbf p}$ has eigenvalues $+1$ and $-1$, so $E=\pm|\mathbf p|.$ In this two-component theory, positive energy has the Pauli degree of freedom aligned with momentum, while negative energy has it anti-aligned. The alignment is locked; it is not an independently adjustable spin direction for a fixed energy sign.

There are many equivalent representations. A unitary change of spinor basis changes the entries of all the matrices without changing any physical prediction. What matters is the abstract set of relations $\{\alpha_i,\alpha_j\}=2\delta_{ij}\mathbb{1},
\qquad
\{\alpha_i,\beta\}=0,
\qquad
\beta^2=\mathbb{1}.$

p.src:

\sigma_i&0\\
0&-\sigma_i
\end{pmatrix},

\beta=
\begin{pmatrix}
0&I_2\\
I_2&0
\end{pmatrix}.$ The Pauli matrices in the diagonal blocks guarantee that different $\alpha_i$ anti-commute. The off-diagonal identity blocks in $\beta$ guarantee that $\beta$ anti-commutes with every $\alpha_i$.

p.src: Chirality and the Meaning of the Extra Components

u.src: Chirality and the Meaning of the Extra Components
en: Chirality and the Meaning of the Extra Components

p.src: What physical distinction did the enlargement add? Start with the massless upper block, $H_R=\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\mathbf P,$ and the massless lower block, $H_L=-\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\mathbf P.$ For positive-energy states, the first has spin aligned with momentum and the second has spin anti-aligned. These are opposite helicities. In a massless theory helicity is invariant under proper Lorentz transformations, because no observer can overtake a lightlike particle and reverse its momentum while leaving its spin unchanged. The two blocks therefore describe opposite chiral sectors.

u.src: The Alpha Matrices Are Velocity, Not Spin
en: The Alpha Matrices Are Velocity, Not Spin

p.src: Each $\alpha_i$ has two $+1$ eigenvalues and two $-1$ eigenvalues. Different components do not commute, so they cannot all be measured sharply at once. To identify what one component represents, use the Heisenberg equation. For an operator $L$ without explicit time dependence, $\dot L=i[H,L].$ The sign convention is fixed here by the Schrödinger evolution $e^{-iHt}$.

p.src:
Apply Eq.  to the position operator $x$. The matrices act on spinor indices and commute with position, while only $P_x$ fails to commute with $x$: $\begin{aligned}
\dot x
&=i[\boldsymbol{\alpha}\cdot\mathbf P+\beta m,x]\\
&=i\alpha_x[P_x,x]\\
&=\alpha_x,
\end{aligned}$ because $[P_x,x]=-i$. Thus $\alpha_x$ is the $x$-component of the velocity operator; similarly, $\dot{\mathbf x}=\boldsymbol{\alpha}.$

p.src: The velocity is not conserved: $\dot\alpha_x=i[H,\alpha_x]\ne0.$ The terms containing $\alpha_y$, $\alpha_z$, and $\beta$ fail to commute with $\alpha_x$. A state containing both positive- and negative-energy components consequently displays a rapid oscillatory contribution to its position. This is zitterbewegung, literally trembling motion.

p.src: The vacuum cannot merely mean a state with no particles. It must be the state from which no further energy can be removed. If an empty state allows us to add a negative-energy particle, lower the energy, add another, and continue indefinitely, then that empty state is not a stable vacuum.

p.src: Fermi statistics supplies a historical way out. Place one electron in every negative-energy state. Each added electron lowers the total energy, but exclusion allows only one electron in each one-particle state. Once every negative-energy state is filled, no additional electron can fall into that sector. Dirac identified this filled configuration as the vacuum.

p.src: A Hole Is a Positron

u.src: A Hole Is a Positron
en: A Hole Is a Positron

p.src: With all negative-energy states occupied, two kinds of excitation are possible. We may add a positive-energy electron above the sea. Or we may remove one negative-energy electron and leave a hole.

p.src: A hole has the opposite charge of the missing electron. Removing charge $-e$ changes the charge by $+e$. It also has positive excitation energy. If the removed electron had $E_-<0$, then the energy measured relative to the filled vacuum changes by $E_{\mathrm{hole}}=-E_->0.$ The hole is a positive-energy, positively charged excitation: the positron.

In a time-ordered diagram it is conventional to draw electron-number flow upward for the electron and the positron line with the opposite arrow. The arrows track fermion-number or charge flow; they are not little classical velocity vectors.

p.src: One Fermion Field Contains Electrons and Positrons

u.src: One Fermion Field Contains Electrons and Positrons
en: One Fermion Field Contains Electrons and Positrons

p.src:
The field operator brings the historical picture into modern algebra. Suppress spinor indices, normalization factors, and time dependence for the moment. A one-dimensional field may be expanded schematically as $\psi(x)
\sim
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dp\,a(p)e^{ipx}.$ For the right-moving dispersion $E=p$, positive $p$ labels positive energy and negative $p$ labels negative energy. Split the integral: $\psi(x)
\sim
\int_0^\infty dp\,a(p)e^{ipx}
+
\int_{-\infty}^0 dp\,a(p)e^{ipx}.$ In the second term set $p=-q$, with $q>0$, and reinterpret annihilation of a filled negative-energy electron as creation of a positron: $b^\dagger(q):=a(-q).$ Then $\psi(x)
\sim
\int_0^\infty dp\,
\left[
a(p)e^{ipx}
+
b^\dagger(p)e^{-ipx}
\right].$ The exact signs of the plane-wave phases depend on the spacetime convention; the invariant content is that $\psi$ contains an electron annihilator and a positron creator.

p.src: The historical sea remains useful because its logic has a close condensed-matter analogue. In a crystal, a fixed number of electrons fill the lowest available one-particle states up to the Fermi level. The filled ground state is not empty. Promoting one electron above that level leaves an unoccupied state below it. Relative to the filled background, the hole carries positive excitation energy and can behave as a positive charge carrier.
